newsitem.title: FRANCE: Rhone plans $4.3 billion Rorer buyout.
newsitem.headline: Rhone plans $4.3 billion Rorer buyout.

text.p: French drug and chemical maker Rhone-Poulenc said Thursday it planned to launch a 25 billion franc ($4.3 billion) bid for the rest of U.S. drug company Rhone-Poulenc Rorer, in which it already holds a 68.3 percent stake.
Rhone-Poulenc said it would pay Rhone-Poulenc Rorer's shareholders $92 a share in the deal. RPR stock jumped $11.375 to $90.875 on the New York Stock Exchange.

The French company also said it would combine its chemical and fiber operations into a single unit that would be partly spun off and taken public in 1998. It said it would retain control of the new unit but did not give details.
The moves are aimed at boosting Rhone-Poulenc's competitive muscle in the fast-changing global chemical and pharmaceutical industry, which has been swept by a wave of big mergers.
"The logic is clear," said Rhone-Poulenc Chairman Jean-Rene Fourtou. "It is to become a strong worldwide company in life sciences."
He said the buyout of RPR, which is based in Collegeville, Pa., would give Rhone-Poulenc the means for future expansion.

"Our developement is internally based, but we do not exclude in time participating in other strategic movements. This deal allows us to envision movements that until now would have been impossible," Fourtou told a news conference.
"Alliances are just starting to happen in the chemicals sector. Greater autonomy should allow (the new company) to participate...if the opportunity presents itself."

Fourtou, answering speculation that the spin-off could be the first step to exiting the chemicals business, said Rhone-Poulenc was committed to speciality chemicals and would not sell off the new unit.
He said the only risks to completing the deal were a rise in the RPR share price to more than $92 or the collapse of the French stock market, both of which he said were unlikely.
But U.S. analysts predicted that Rhone-Poulenc may have to raise its offer.
"I think the deal will not get done at $92, that it will go higher, perhaps as high at $110 a share," said Rodman and Renshaw analyst James Keeney in New York.
The revamping of Rhone's chemical and fiber divisions would occur regardless of the outcome of its offer for RPR.
Rhone-Poulenc shareholders cheered the news, bidding the stock up sharply. It rose 19 percent to 252.50 francs ($43.30).
The company's stock price has been held back by its wide array of businesses, and analysts said they expected the share price to continue to rise.
"I am very positive because the P-E ratio will automatically rise and because the company will look more like a true pharmaceutical company," said one analyst in Paris.
Rhone Poulenc Managing Director Igor Landau said the takeover "is a little dilutive the first year, a little less the second and not at all, on the contrary, from year three."
In 1996, Rhone Poulenc earned 2.74 billion francs ($470 million) or 8.44 francs a share, compared with 6.71 francs in 1995.
